evidence.paraphrase: The magic shoes are explained as instantly transporting the wearer to any place, time, or state of being they wish for.
evidence.quote: These shoes possess the property of instantly transporting him who has them on to the place or the period in which he most wishes to be; every wish, as regards time or place, or state of being, will be immediately fulfilled

evidence.paraphrase: The Councillor is transported back in time to the era of King Hans, finding an older, unpaved Copenhagen.
evidence.quote: By the magic power of the shoes he was carried back to the times of King Hans; on which account his foot very naturally sank in the mud and puddles of the street, there having been in those days no pavement in Copenhagen.

evidence.paraphrase: The familiar modern street has been replaced by wooden, thatched-roof houses of an earlier age.
evidence.quote: He gazed at the street formerly so well known to him, and now so strange in appearance, and looked at the houses more attentively: most of them were of wood, slightly put together; and many had a thatched roof.

evidence.paraphrase: The displaced Councillor reacts with confusion, suspecting illusion or drunkenness.
evidence.quote: "I either behold a fata morgana, or I am regularly tipsy," whimpered out the Councillor. "But what's this?"

evidence.paraphrase: The Councillor offers a scientific explanation of meteors as reflections of the aurora, caused by electricity.
evidence.quote:
Such meteorous appearances are to be explained in this way
can the reflections of the Aurora Borealis, and it is highly probable they are caused principally by electricity.

evidence.paraphrase: The shoes cause the watchman to take on the identity, thoughts, and feelings of the lieutenant.
evidence.quote: In the same moment the watchman was again watchman. It was the shoes that caused the metamorphosis by means of which, unknown to himself, he took upon him the thoughts and feelings of the officer

evidence.paraphrase: The narrator explains the speed of light and electricity, framing the soul's travel as carried by electricity.
evidence.quote: It flies nineteen million times faster than the best race-horse; and yet electricity is quicker still. Death is an electric shock which our heart receives; the freed soul soars upwards on the wings of electricity.

evidence.paraphrase: The watchman's spirit travels to the moon in seconds, arriving at a soft, lightweight lunar landscape.
evidence.quote: In a few seconds the watchman had done the fifty-two thousand of our miles up to the moon, which, as everyone knows, was formed out of matter much lighter than our earth; and is, so we should say, as soft as newly-fallen snow.

evidence.paraphrase: The moon-dwellers debate whether Earth can be inhabited, doubting its atmosphere suits rational life.
evidence.quote: The Selenites disputed variously about our earth, and expressed their doubts if it could be inhabited: the air, they said, must certainly be too dense to allow any rational dweller in the moon the necessary free respiration.

evidence.paraphrase: While his spirit is on the moon, the watchman's body is found dead in the street.
evidence.quote: the supposed sleeper lost his balance, the body lay motionless, stretched out on the pavement: the man was dead.

evidence.paraphrase: The clerk's wish causes his head to slip through the railings instantly, trapping his body.
evidence.quote: "Would to Heaven I had got my head through!" said he, involuntarily; and instantly through it slipped, easily and without pain, notwithstanding it was pretty large and thick.

evidence.paraphrase: The shoes shrink the clerk and send him journeying literally through the hearts of the audience.
evidence.quote: And behold! to the Shoes of Fortune this was the cue; the whole man shrunk together and a most uncommon journey through the hearts of the front row of spectators, now began.

evidence.paraphrase: The clerk is transformed into a bird, his clothes becoming feathers and wings.
evidence.quote: He had hardly uttered these hasty words when the skirts and sleeves of his coat folded themselves together into wings; the clothes became feathers, and the galoshes claws.

evidence.paraphrase: The young Divine is instantly transported to Switzerland, traveling in a cramped coach.
evidence.quote: In short, he was travelling. He was in the middle of Switzerland, but packed up with eight other passengers in the inside of an eternally-creaking diligence

evidence.paraphrase: A wish transports the Divine instantly across the Alps to Italy.
evidence.quote: And so saying he was on the other side in Italy, between Florence and Rome.

evidence.paraphrase: The Divine's wish for the highest happiness fulfills itself as death, leaving him in a coffin.
evidence.quote: And as he spoke the word he was again in his home; the long white curtains hung down from the windows, and in the middle of the floor stood the black coffin; in it he lay in the sleep of death. His wish was fulfilled

evidence.paraphrase: The narrator contrasts the reader's familiar steam travel with the far greater velocity of light.
evidence.quote: As to ourselves, we all know the speed produced by the employment of steam; we have experienced it either on railroads, or in boats when crossing the sea; but such a flight is like the travelling of a sloth in comparison with the velocity with which light moves.

evidence.paraphrase: The revived watchman describes his lunar experience as the worst ordeal of his life.
evidence.quote: "He asserted that the preceding night had been the worst that ever the malice of fate had allotted him; he would not for two silver marks again go through what he had endured while moon-stricken"

evidence.paraphrase: The lunar terrain is described with reference to a real astronomical map of the moon.
evidence.quote: He found himself on one of the many circumjacent mountain-ridges with which we are acquainted by means of Dr. Madler's "Map of the Moon."
